# Using the acceptance dynamics

With a defined simulation framework, one can begin to formulate
precisely how to use the acceptance dynamics. The core idea is
that if the bias exists or is economically relevant it should
be observable in some manner and if so we can try to minimize
the bias. Based on this hypothesis one can then formulate
a scenario, using that we have full knowledge of the applicants' population,
which allows gathering evidence on the plausibility of such hypothesis.
Having delivered this evidence, a reward signal is defined along to a formulation
of the RI problem as a reinforcement learning problem.

## Hypothesis definition

To formalize the statement "the bias should be observable and can be minimized"
we need to first formulate what is understood as bias and how one can
observe it. First I define what I understand as observable bias, which I call surprise.
Second, a theoretical motivation is presented of when this bias should
*not* be observable, that gives an intuition of the plausibility of the observability
of the bias. Third, I give some simulation based evidence of my claims on observability
of the bias.

### Surprise signal

It is well known that biased samples lead to biased evaluation of classifiers in the sense
that is the performance is not representative on how the classifier performs on unseen data
[@sugiyama2007covariate], as sampling bias results in covariate shifts. Most of the literature
on this topic has a focus on the bias as measured on an unseen unbiased sample. However, I
believe that this bias is also observed on the population of accepted applicants, and it
can be used as an informative signal.

My claim is that this bias is also observable on the accepted applicants as well. This means
that the expected performance of a scorecard as evaluated on accepts does not correspond to the
observed performance on accepted applicants of the next round. Then, I define the surprise
$\eta^{(t)}$ at acceptance round $t$ analogously to the definition of evaluation bias, namely
as the difference between expected performance $m_{CV}$ measured by a metric $m$ generated through
CV on historical data and the realized performance on the new unseen data of the accepts.
$$
\eta^{(t)} := m_{CV}\left(\mathbf{X}_m^{:t}, \mathbf{Y}^{:t}\right) - m\left(\mathbf{X}_m^{(t)}, \mathbf{Y}^{(t)}\right)
$$

### An unsurprising setting

The claim on observability of the bias only on the accepted population
is strong and should be justified. Therefore, I propose here a realistic
setting for FIs with high volume of credits for which from a theoretical
perspective one could hope to only find small values of $\eta^{(t)}$ when
ignoring the missing data mechanism. The purpose here is not mathematical
rigourosity, but an intuition on the theoretical foundations to assume that
the bias is observable as surprise.

The most general case that still allows for unbiasedly estimated scorecards
is MAR as defined on @eq-mar-only-model. Given the existence of
regularity conditions ensuring well-defined joint and marginal densities
(as in @sec-app-population-simulation) the MAR condition implies
$$
Z^{(t)} \perp\!\!\!\perp Y^{:t} \big | X^{:t}
$$
which, almost everywhere, leads to
$$
p_{Y | X}(y, x) = p_{Y | X, Z^{:t}=\alpha}(y, x)
$${#eq-Y-cond-X-density-indep-Z}

with $y \in \{g, b\}, x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha \in \{a, r\}$. Suppose
the following conditions hold:

1. The number of applicants $N_t$ is sufficiently large at
   each round, so that many applicants are accepted, i.e. *high volume of credits*.
2. The scorecard *estimation algorithm remains unchanged* across rounds, i. e.
   $\ell_t = \ell_{t'}$, $t, t' \in \mathbf{T}$, 
3. The *estimation method is unbiased* in the sense of this thesis, {#item-assumption-estimation-method-unbiased}
4. The *cutoff* $c_t$ is *chosen consistently* across rounds optimizing discriminatory
   power (e.g., fixed ROC point) {#item-assumption-c-t-consistent-discriminatory}
5. The missing data process satisfies the *MAR assumption*, meaning $f_h = 0$ and
   $Z^{(t)}_i$ is fully determined by $\hat{s}_t, c_t$ and $X^{(t)}_{m, i}$
   for $t \in \mathbf{T}, i \in \{1, \ldots, N_t\}$ $Z^{(t)}_i$^[Recall
   @eq-Z-t-with-threshold-and-scorecard-no-overwrites].

Under this assumptions and considering that the applicants population distribution
is time invariant, one can expect the distribution of the accepted applicants at each
round to be approximately the same. To describe this distribution first let
$$
A_t := \left\{
    x \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m} \middle | \hat{s}_t(x) > c_t
\right\}
$$
denote the acceptance region under the assumptions above. Then the applicants distribution
conditioned on acceptance can be defined for any measurable set
$E \in 2^{E_Y} \otimes \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^f\right)$ as
$$
\mathbb{P}_{Y, X | X \in A_t}(E) = 
\frac{
    \mathbb{P}\left((Y, X) \in E, X \in A_t \right)
}{
    \mathbb{P}\left(X \in A_t \right)
}.
$$

Now, $A_t$ has a theoretical optimal (cost unaware) counterpart, namely
$$
A = \left\{
    x \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m} \middle | s^*(x) > c
\right\},
$$
with
$$
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m}:
\operatorname{sign}(s^*(x) - c) = \operatorname{sign}(\mathbb{P}(Y=g | X = x) - 0.5)
$$
i. e. the feature region corresponding to repayment being more likely than
default. Since the choosing of $c_t$ optimizes discriminatory power
(assumption @item-assumption-c-t-consistent-discriminatory), and $\hat{s}_t$ is
estimated unbiasedely (assumption @item-assumption-estimation-method-unbiased),
one can conjecture that these objects converge (e.g. in probability) to their
optimal counterparts $s*$ and $c$.^[
    Note: This claim requires the training sample coming from the first acceptance
    round (so at $t=1$) to be i.i.d. and to be MAR so that consistency arguments
    for e.g. ML based estimators can hold. Through the proportionality of
    $s*$ to $p_{Y=b | X}(x)$ from @eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes and the i.i.d. ness
    of the applicants population at time step, one could make an argument using
    a theorem like Glivenko-Cantelli. However, since we are working with certain
    regions of the distribution of $X_m$, this argument would be lengthy, difficult
    and would be outside of the scope of the thesis.
]

With the convergence of the cut-off and the scorecard we would obtain a convergence
in measure of $A_t \overset{\mathbb{P}_{X_m}}{\longrightarrow} A$.

there should be almost everywhere a pointwise convergence of the scorecard
with growing $N_t$ in the sense
$$
\operatorname{sign}\left(\hat{s}_t(x) - c \right) \to \operatorname{sign}\left(\mathbb{P}(Y = g | X_m = x) - 0.5 \right), x \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m}
$$

because of which $A_t$ should converge in measure to towards $A$ w.r.t.
$\mathbb{P}_{X_m}$. From this convergence one could then argue a convergence
in distribution
$$
\mathbb{P}_{Y, X | X \in A_t} \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}_{Y, X | X \in A}
$$ {#eq-convergence-accepted-applicants}

If @eq-convergence-accepted-applicants, one could and should expect that
$\hat{s}_t$ would perform the same in evaluation as well as in new accepts,
regardless of the covariate shift with respect to the full population.
